Regio-, Stereo-, and Enantioselective Copper-Catalyzed Allylation of
Sulﬁnylamines with Allenes
Jie Zhu, Yue Zhao, Shengming Ma,* and Minyan Wang*
Abstract: Sulﬁnamides, pivotal scaffolds in modern organic synthesis, have undergone a continuous evolution of synthetic
methodologies over the past century, yet the precise construction of sulfur stereocenters remains a signiﬁcant synthetic
challenge. Herein, we report a versatile catalytic asymmetric strategy for the synthesis of S-chirogenic allyl sulﬁnamides
through the direct allylation of sulﬁnylamines with allenes. Our methodology employs a catalytic system comprising copper
salts, hydrosilanes, and readily accessible chiral ligands, which facilitates the in situ generation of organocopper surrogates
via hydrocupration of allenes. This approach demonstrates remarkable substrate scope and excellent regio-, stereo-, and
enantioselectivity across a diverse array of sulﬁnamide products. Comprehensive mechanistic investigations, including
detailed experimental studies and computational analyses, have been conducted to elucidate the reaction pathway and
identify the key factors governing enantioselectivity.
Chiral sulﬁnamides featuring stereogenic S(IV) centers have
garnered particular attention as pivotal synthetic targets. [1–15]
These compounds not only function as crucial intermediates
for the stereoselective assembly of sulfur-containing func-
tional groups [16–19] but also exhibit remarkable versatility
as bifunctional reagents under mild photoredox catalysis
conditions.[20,21] Among these, the synthesis of chiral S-
allyl sulﬁnamides has garnered signiﬁcant attention due to
their intricate structural complexity and diverse applications.
A landmark achievement in 1990 facilitated the enantiop-
ure synthesis of S-allyl sulﬁnamides via ene reactions of
trans-alkenes with N-sulﬁnylcarbamates derived from chiral
alcohols (Figure 1a).[22] T o eliminate the reliance on chiral
auxiliaries, Beyah and colleagues in 2017 pioneered an
asymmetric catalytic variant, employing a chiral antimony
catalyst in the ene-type sulﬁnamidation of cis- alkenes
(Figure 1b).[23] However, the propensity of the N-sulfonyl

Sulﬁnylamines (R–NSO), distinguished by their orthogo-
nal cumulative π -systems, have emerged as pivotal building
blocks in organic synthesis, facilitating a diverse range of
chemical transformations. [24,25] The nucleophilic addition of
magnesium reagents to sulﬁnylamines, developed in 1974,
offers a direct method for synthesizing S-allyl sulﬁnamides, as
well as a broad range of other sulﬁnamides (Figure 1c).[26–28]
Subsequent catalytic advancements have aimed at enhancing
compatibility with sensitive functional groups by employing
readily accessible alkyl[29,30] and aryl[31] feedstocks in addition
reactions. The advent of asymmetric catalysis utilizing aryl
boron compounds [32,33] or halides [34–37] with sulﬁnylamines
has introduced novel pathways for the synthesis of chiral
sulﬁnamides. Inspired by these developments, we propose an
enantioselective nucleophilic addition of allylmetal species to
sulﬁnylamines to establish an S-stereogenic center. Here, we
present an asymmetric catalytic allylation of sulﬁnylamines
for the synthesis of enantioenriched S-allyl sulﬁnamides with
excellent regio-, stereo-, and enantioselectivity (Figure 1d).
Our strategy leverages copper salts, hydrosilanes, and com-
mercially available ligands to in situ generate allylcopper
nucleophiles from allenes with high regio- and stereoselectiv-
ity through hydrocupration. [38–68] Mechanistic investigations
reveal that the formation of the enantioenriched S-allyl
sulﬁnamides is achieved through the migratory insertion of
the allylcopper nucleophile into the sulﬁnimine, rather than
via a chair-like Zimmerman-T raxler transition state.[69,70] This
approach not only enhances the synthetic efﬁciency but
also broadens the scope of accessible chiral sulﬁnamides,
paving the way for further exploration in sulfur-centered
stereochemistry. Our investigation commenced with the uti-
lization of allene 1a with N-sulﬁnyltritylamine ( I)a st h e
model substrates (T able1). We initially established a reaction

atmosphere. This preliminary setup afforded the target trans
product 1b in a modest 27% yield with an enantiomeric
ratio (er) of 55/45 (entry 1). No rearrangement-type branched
byproducts were observed. Subsequent ligand optimization
revealed signiﬁcant improvements. Switching to BINAP ( L2)
enhanced the yield to 37% with an improved er of 60/40
(entry 2). The introduction of JosiPhos ( L3) further reﬁned
the er to 63/37 (entry 3). A more pronounced enhancement in
enantioselectivity was observed upon substituting the phenyl
groups on the phosphorus of JosiPhos with 3,5-CF 3-Ph groups
(L4), which escalated the er to 85/15 while maintaining high
yield (entry 4). However, replacing PCy 2 with P tBu2 (L5)
resulted in a slight decline in both yield and enantioselectivity
(entry 5). The use of ligand L6, featuring bulky electron-
donating aryl groups on the phosphorus atom, led to a notable
decrease in both yield and enantioselectivity (entry 6). The
choice of solvent emerged as a critical factor for achieving
high enantioselectivity. Employing dioxolane as the solvent
yielded comparable enantioselectivity but reduced the yield
to 30% (entry 7). Conversely, MTBE as the solvent not only
improved the enantioselectivity to 87/13 er but also increased
the yield to 87% (entry 8). Exploration of alternative copper
sources, such as MesCu and TcCu, proved beneﬁcial, with
TcCu notably enhancing the yield to 89% with an er of
88/12 (entries 9 and 10). V arious silane variants were also
tested. DPS displayed relevant reactivity, while TES produced
product 1b with an er of 90/10 and a yield of 74% (entries
11 and 12). Further optimization revealed that lowering
the reaction temperature enhanced the reaction outcome
(entries 13 and 14). Remarkably, reducing the temperature
to −60 °C resulted in an outstanding er of 95/5 and a
yield of 80% (entry 15). Under these conditions, substituting
TES with DEMS also yielded comparable results (entry
16). Reducing the catalyst loading to 5 mol% decreased
conversion but preserved enantioselectivity (entry 17). Con-
trol experiments highlighted the indispensable role of the
copper catalyst, as its omission completely halted the reaction
(entry 18).
In our pursuit to comprehensively explore the reactivity
and structural diversity of allenes, we conducted a systematic
series of experiments utilizing sulﬁnylamine I as the key reac-
tant partner (T able2). Our investigation commenced with the
evaluation of allene 2a and its methyl-substituted analogues
(2a–7a), followed by ethyl ( 8a), isopropyl ( 9a), tert-butyl
(10a), and phenyl ( 11a) derivatives, all of which successfully
yielded the corresponding products ( 2b–11b) with remark-
able efﬁciency. Signiﬁcantly, allenes bearing diverse ether
functionalities on the benzene core ( 12a–17a) demonstrated
exceptional reactivity, delivering the target products 12b–
17b with notably high enantioselectivities. The compatibility

with ﬂuorine ( 18a–21a), chlorine ( 22a), and bromine ( 23a)
derivatives exhibiting minimal interference in the reaction
outcomes while maintaining superior enantioselectivity. Our
experimental results further conﬁrmed the remarkable com-

and OCF 2H( 27a), under the optimized reaction conditions.
The treatment of naphthalene and dibenzo[ b,d]thiophene-
containing allenes ( 26a–28a) proceeded with commendable
efﬁciency, yielding products ( 26b–28b) with excellent enan-
tioselectivity. A particularly signiﬁcant advancement was
achieved in the successful transformation of 1,1-disubstituted
allenes 29a–37a featuring methyl and aryl moieties, which
afforded products 29b–37b with an exceptional enantiose-
lectivity and Z/E selectivity. T o unambiguously determine
the stereochemical outcome, we performed X-ray crystal-
lographic analysis on product 34b,[71] which conclusively
established its E,R-conﬁguration. Expanding the substrate
scope further, we demonstrated the exceptional chemoselec-
tivity of the reaction towards naphthyl ( 38a), long-chain alkyl
(39a), and cyclic ( 40a) allenes, which exclusively yielded the
desired products 38b–40b under the optimized conditions.
T o demonstrate the synthetic versatility of our method,
we conducted comprehensive experiments (Scheme 1). Ini-
tially, this approach’s utility was highlighted through a
1.0 mmol-scale synthesis and subsequent transformations. The
reaction using allene 1a and sulﬁnylamine I as substrates was
smoothly executed, yielding product 1b in 68% yield without
any loss of enantioselectivity. Subsequently, the deprotection
experiment was performed. T reatment of sulﬁnamide 1b with
methanesulfonic acid led to the deprotection product 41 in
71% yield, maintaining the enantioselectivity. Hydrogenation
of 1b with a Pd/C catalyst produced alkyl-sulﬁnamide 42 in
80% yield with 94/6 er.
T o gain deeper insights into the reaction pathway, we
conducted extensive mechanistic studies as depicted in

L4 and TcCu were combined, the copper complex 43 was
formed, as conﬁrmed by X-ray analysis [71] (Scheme 2a).
Utilizing this complex as a catalyst in the reaction between
substrates 1a and I produced results of comparable efﬁcacy,
strongly suggesting that this complex serves as the active
catalytic species. A clear linear relationship was observed
when compounds 1a and I were reacted using L4 as the chiral

T o further investigate the mechanism, we conducted
deuterium labeling experiments (Scheme 2b). When Ph 2SiD2
reagent was used instead of (EtO) 3SiH with allene 1a or
34a, the D atoms were completely transferred to the central
carbon of the allene, suggesting that the Cu-D species
inserts at this position. Finally, the inﬂuence of different N-
substituents on the sulﬁnylamines was examined (Scheme 2c).
Sulﬁnylamines with Ts ( II)a n dP h( III) substituents did
not yield the desired products 1c and 1d. Although the
use of sulﬁnylamines bearing sterically hindered Ad ( IV),
TIPS (V), and SiPh 3 (VI) groups produced small amounts of
products 1e–g, the enantioselectivity was low. These ﬁndings
suggest that the choice of sulﬁnylamine I is advantageous for
achieving both high reactivity and stereoselectivity. Notably,
allene 1a undergoes allylation with ketone 44 under the
current reaction conditions, exclusively yielding the branched
product 45 (Scheme 2d).[72–79] The notable regioselectivity
difference underscores the distinct reactivity between ketones
and sulﬁnylamines. Ketone 44 has an electrophilicity index
of 0.929 eV , much lower than sulﬁnylamine’s 1.219 eV .
This higher index in sulﬁnylamine I reﬂects its stronger
electrophilic nature, boosting its ability to attract electrons in
reactions. Furthermore, the frontier molecular orbital theory
is used to explain the different selectivities of the reaction (see
Supporting Information for details).

density functional theory (DFT) was then performed to

illustrated in Supporting Information . Initially, the copper(I)

active catalyst 43. When silane is introduced into the system,

with the allene, leading to the formation of diverse types

can also be well controlled (4.9 kcal mol −1 for TS3A-E-

are primarily attributed to the substantial steric hindrance
between the phenyl group and the alkenyl hydrogen in both
TS3A-Z and TS3A-Z-29a .
Furthermore, we investigated the allylation reactions of
INT2A and INT3A-E with sulﬁnylamine I, respectively
(Figure 3). The coordination of N and O atoms of sulﬁny-
lamine into intermediate INT2A can form INT3A-N and
INT3A-O, respectively. Due to the relatively higher calcu-
lated energy for INT3B-N, we excluded the reaction pathway
involving this intermediate. The allylation reaction that
proceeds through the six-membered chair-like Zimmerman-
T raxler transition state TS3B-linear-R has an energy barrier
of 11.8 kcal mol −1. Although this pathway is more kinetically
favorable than the direct allylation route leading to branched
products, its energy requirement remains signiﬁcantly higher
than that of the 1,3-copper migration process of INT2A via
transition states TS3A-E. These computational results imply
that INT2A exhibits a distinct preference for undergoing
transformation to yield INT3A-E, rather than participating
in an allylation reaction with sulﬁnylamine. The migratory
insertion between intermediate INT3A-E and sulﬁnylamine
I is the crucial step dictating both the regio- and enantio-
selectivity within the catalytic cycle. The migratory insertion
reaction of the S ═N bond through the transition state
TS4A-linear-R manifests a pronounced kinetic favorability.
Speciﬁcally, the energy barrier associated with this pathway
is 2.8 kcal mol −1 lower than that of the analogous reaction
pathway via the transition state TS4A-linear-S (4.0 kcal mol−1
versus 6.8 kcal mol −1). This distinct energy disparity leads
to a greater tendency for the product to form in the R-
conﬁguration. The selective migratory insertion of the S ═O
double bond into intermediate INT3A-E occurs via the
transition states TS4B-R and TS4B-S, with activation energies
of 8.2 and 5.4 kcal/mol, respectively. These values are sub-
stantially higher than the activation energies associated with
the migratory insertion involving the S ═N double bond. T o
gain deeper insights into the enantioselectivity observed in the
migratory insertion process, the independent gradient model
based on Hirshfeld partitioning (IGMH) was utilized to

In conclusion, this study establishes a robust and versatile
copper-catalyzed platform for the stereoselective synthesis
of chiral S-allyl sulﬁnamides, addressing a long-standing
challenge in asymmetric sulfur chemistry. The developed
methodology demonstrates remarkable functional group tol-
erance and substrate scope, enabling the efﬁcient coupling
of diverse allenes with sulﬁnylamines under mild reductive
conditions. Through a synergistic combination of experi-
mental investigations and computational analyses, we have
elucidated the intricate reaction mechanism and identiﬁed
key factors governing the selective aryl addition processes.
Given the growing recognition of chiral S-stereogenic com-
pounds as privileged structural motifs in pharmaceutical
development and agrochemical innovation, we anticipate
that this catalytic system will ﬁnd broad applications in the
synthesis of biologically active molecules.

Regio-, Stereo-, and Enantioselective Copper-Catalyzed Allylation of
Sulfinylamines with Allenes
Jie Zhu, Yue Zhao, Shengming Ma,* and Minyan Wang*

Abstract: Sulfinamides, pivotal scaffolds in modern organic synthesis, have undergone a continuous evolution of synthetic
methodologies over the past century, yet the precise construction of sulfur stereocenters remains a significant synthetic
challenge. Herein, we report a versatile catalytic asymmetric strategy for the synthesis of S-chirogenic allyl sulfinamides
through the direct allylation of sulfinylamines with allenes. Our methodology employs a catalytic system comprising copper
salts, hydrosilanes, and readily accessible chiral ligands, which facilitates the in situ generation of organocopper surrogates
via hydrocupration of allenes. This approach demonstrates remarkable substrate scope and excellent regio-, stereo-, and
enantioselectivity across a diverse array of sulfinamide products. Comprehensive mechanistic investigations, including
detailed experimental studies and computational analyses, have been conducted to elucidate the reaction pathway and
identify the key factors governing enantioselectivity.

Chiral sulfinamides featuring stereogenic S(IV) centers have
garnered particular attention as pivotal synthetic targets.<sup>[1–15]</sup>
These compounds not only function as crucial intermediates
for the stereoselective assembly of sulfur-containing func-
tional groups<sup>[16–19]</sup> but also exhibit remarkable versatility
as bifunctional reagents under mild photoredox catalysis
conditions.<sup>[20,21]</sup> Among these, the synthesis of chiral S-
allyl sulfinamides has garnered significant attention due to
their intricate structural complexity and diverse applications.
A landmark achievement in 1990 facilitated the enantiop-
ure synthesis of S-allyl sulfinamides via ene reactions of
trans-alkenes with N-sulfinylcarbamates derived from chiral
alcohols (Figure 1a).<sup>[22]</sup> To eliminate the reliance on chiral
auxiliaries, Beyah and colleagues in 2017 pioneered an
asymmetric catalytic variant, employing a chiral antimony
catalyst in the ene-type sulfinamidation of cis- alkenes
(Figure 1b).<sup>[23]</sup> However, the propensity of the N-sulfonyl
sulfur-centered chirality, highlighting the necessity for more

robust sulfinamide moiety to act as a leaving group, has
limited its utility in adaptable synthetic methodologies.

Sulfinylamines (R–NSO), distinguished by their orthogo-
nal cumulative π-systems, have emerged as pivotal building
blocks in organic synthesis, facilitating a diverse range of
chemical transformations.<sup>[24,25]</sup> The nucleophilic addition of
magnesium reagents to sulfinylamines, developed in 1974,
offers a direct method for synthesizing S-allyl sulfinamides, as
well as a broad range of other sulfinamides (Figure 1c).<sup>[26–28]</sup>
Subsequent catalytic advancements have aimed at enhancing
compatibility with sensitive functional groups by employing
readily accessible alkyl<sup>[29,30]</sup> and aryl<sup>[31]</sup> feedstocks in addition
reactions. The advent of asymmetric catalysis utilizing aryl
boron compounds<sup>[32,33]</sup> or halides<sup>[34–37]</sup> with sulfinylamines
has introduced novel pathways for the synthesis of chiral
sulfinamides. Inspired by these developments, we propose an
enantioselective nucleophilic addition of allylmetal species to
sulfinylamines to establish an S-stereogenic center. Here, we
present an asymmetric catalytic allylation of sulfinylamines
for the synthesis of enantioenriched S-allyl sulfinamides with
excellent regio-, stereo-, and enantioselectivity (Figure 1d).
Our strategy leverages copper salts, hydrosilanes, and com-
mercially available ligands to in situ generate allylcopper
nucleophiles from allenes with high regio- and stereoselectiv-
ity through hydrocupration.<sup>[38–68]</sup> Mechanistic investigations
reveal that the formation of the enantioenriched S-allyl
sulfinamides is achieved through the migratory insertion of
the allylcopper nucleophile into the sulfinimine, rather than
via a chair-like Zimmerman-Traxler transition state.<sup>[69,70]</sup> This
approach not only enhances the synthetic efficiency but
also broadens the scope of accessible chiral sulfinamides,
paving the way for further exploration in sulfur-centered
stereochemistry. Our investigation commenced with the uti-
lization of allene 1a with N-sulfinyltritylamine (I) as the
model substrates (Table 1). We initially established a reaction
system employing 10 mol% of Cu(OAc) and 12 mol%

catalyst coordinates with the chiral ligand L4, generating the
active catalyst 43. When silane is introduced into the system,
the active catalyst 43 undergoes a σ-CAM mechanism with
the silane via the transition state TS1A, with an activation

that INT2A exhibits a distinct preference for undergoing
transformation to yield INT3A-E, rather than participating
in an allylation reaction with sulfinylamine. The migratory

configuration. The selective migratory insertion of the S═O
double bond into intermediate INT3A-E occurs via the
transition states TS4B-R and TS4B-S, with activation energies
of 8.2 and 5.4 kcal/mol, respectively. These values are sub-

that in the favorable transition state TS4A-linear-R, stronger
hydrogen-bond interactions exist between the C-H bonds
of the chiral ligand and the oxygen or nitrogen atoms of

In conclusion, this study establishes a robust and versatile
copper-catalyzed platform for the stereoselective synthesis
of chiral S-allyl sulfinamides, addressing a long-standing
challenge in asymmetric sulfur chemistry. The developed
methodology demonstrates remarkable functional group tol-
erance and substrate scope, enabling the efficient coupling
of diverse allenes with sulfinylamines under mild reductive
conditions. Through a synergistic combination of experi-
mental investigations and computational analyses, we have
elucidated the intricate reaction mechanism and identified
key factors governing the selective aryl addition processes.
Given the growing recognition of chiral S-stereogenic com-
pounds as privileged structural motifs in pharmaceutical
development and agrochemical innovation, we anticipate
that this catalytic system will find broad applications in the
synthesis of biologically active molecules.
